To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
increased CO2 concentrations favor growth of microaerophillic lactobacilli and that these changes are associated with changes in the vaginal epithelial cells transcriptome.
increased CO2 concentrations in the vaginal environment favor the growth of specific lactobacillus species and alter host epithelial gene expression.
increased levels of CO2, a common environmental factor associated with inflammation, favor specific anaerobes and lead to changes in the host epithelium.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the human vaginal ecosystem, a complex environment in which both aerobic and anaerobic bacteria thrive.
defining the impact of the vaginal ecosystem's physiology on the relationships established between host and bacterial communities.

the development of a reproducible, controlled model of the human vaginal mucosal ecosystem that supports the study of the complex interactions that occur between host cells and the bacteria that colonize them.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the vaginal ecosystem modeling system is an effective and useful tool for studying the impact of environmental conditions upon the growth of anaerobic and microaerophillic bacteria in the context of the human host.
the human vaginal mucosa provides an excellent model for study of vaginal bacterial communities in health and disease.

this study supports the need for additional investigation into the impact of environmental changes associated with host health and behavior upon the symbiotic or adversarial relationships established by the microbial communities present in a human vaginal ecosystem.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a model that allows us to study the vaginal ecosystem in a way that is not possible in the living human host.
we are using an ex vivo human mucosa culture system in conjunction with vaginal bacterial communities (VB) to study the impact upon the mucosa of increased CO2 levels.
we have demonstrated a novel approach for the study of the human vagina and its microbiome.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CO2 is a major factor that influences the composition of the VBC community and the host response.
the vaginal ecosystem, as it exists in the human host, can be modeled in a controlled, reproducible ex vivo setting that supports the growth and behavior of anaerobic bacterial communities.
the host's environment can have an effect upon the growth of anaerobic microbes.
